summary: Try block sizes from the biggest down; the first k×k block that looks the same after a 180° rotation is the answer (T15 — brute force + pruning). A cheap corner check throws away most blocks before the full check.

blocks.title: Read the matrix
blocks.text: N on one line; the program prints `Enter matrix elements:` itself, then reads N rows of numbers without a prompt.

blocks.title: Pre-reverse every row once
blocks.text: A 180° rotation reverses the row order AND each row. Storing reversed rows in `REV` up front lets the check read a reversed piece directly, instead of reversing again for every block.

blocks.title: Cheap check: opposite corners
blocks.text: After a 180° turn the top-left cell lands on the bottom-right, so they must be equal. Most blocks fail here immediately, which is what makes brute force fast enough.

blocks.title: Full check: row i vs row k−1−i reversed
blocks.text: Row i of the block must equal row (k−1−i) of the block read backwards. Columns c..c+k−1 of a row appear at positions N−c−k..N−c−1 of its reversed copy, hence the `REV` slice. We only need the top half plus the middle row (`k // 2 + 1`), because the bottom half repeats the same pairs.

blocks.title: All rows matched
blocks.text: If no row pair failed, the block is symmetric.

blocks.title: Biggest size first
blocks.text: Looping k from N down means the first symmetric block found is the largest, so we can stop right there. `return` inside a function exits all three loops at once (a `break` would only leave the innermost one). A 1×1 block is always symmetric, so `return 1` is just a safety net.

complexity: Worst case is many blocks × k² work, but the corner check rejects most blocks at once; a random 250×250 grid ran in about 1.5 s.
pitfalls: Searching small to big — then you can't stop at the first hit.
Only checking the diagonal or one pair of rows.
